opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, people sometimes assume that someone at Yann's level must have stepped back from the day-to-day, that he's mostly a figurehead now, giving keynotes and posting on social media. In my experience at NYU, that's not the picture at all.

He's still very much a scientist at heart. When we talk, it's not at the level of "here's the grand vision, go figure it out." He'll get into the details: the objective function, why a particular architecture collapses, whether a representation is actually capturing something meaningful or just exploiting a shortcut in the data. He has very strong intuitions, and he's been thinking about many of these problems, like self-supervised learning, energy-based models, and world models, for decades. So when a student brings him a result, he can often place it immediately in a much longer history of ideas, and that's incredibly valuable.

He also has very firm opinions, as everyone knows. He's not shy about saying, "I think this direction is a dead end," or "autoregressive LLMs alone won't get us there." But in a research setting that's actually healthy. It forces you to sharpen your own arguments. You can disagree with him, and he's open to debate, as long as you bring evidence or a good argument.

Of course, his time is split across many things, so he isn't writing code or running experiments himself. The students and postdocs do the hands-on work. But in terms of intellectual involvement, setting directions, asking the hard questions, and pushing toward ideas like learning world models from video or joint embedding approaches instead of pixel-level generation, he's still deeply engaged. For a young faculty member like me, having someone like that nearby, who still gets genuinely excited about a new idea, is a big part of what makes the environment special.

r001.rationale: The candidate says LeCun discusses technical details such as objective functions, but does not state that he personally derives equations step by step during group meetings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann is genuinely still hands-on, which surprises people. He's not a figurehead who shows up for the group photo. He reads papers closely, he argues about details, and when we're discussing a result he'll push on the specific experiment, not just the high-level story. At NYU he's been running a lot of the JEPA line of work, the self-supervised, world-model direction, and he's deeply involved in how that's designed, not just what it's called.

What I find most characteristic is that he has a very strong, very stable set of beliefs about what the right path is, and he's willing to be unpopular about it. He's been skeptical of pure autoregressive language models as the route to real intelligence for years, and he keeps building toward the alternative instead of just tweeting about it. That consistency actually matters for students. You know where he stands, so the disagreements are productive.

At the same time, he gives people a lot of room. My group's work on vision, on representation learning, on multimodal models, he doesn't try to steer it. He'll engage with it, he'll challenge it, sometimes he'll tell me he thinks something is a dead end, and then he'll let me go find out for myself. So I'd characterize it as a mix of real technical depth, strong opinions, and a fairly light touch. For a place like NYU, having someone like that around, still arguing about gradients and architectures rather than just strategy, is a big part of why the research culture feels the way it does.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes LeCun as hands-on and technically engaged, but does not say he personally derives equations step by step during group meetings.
